details:
MarsPath is an interactive web prototype that helps users explore the Jezero Crater region of Mars through real scientific imagery and simulated journeys. It connects orbital context with rover photographs and guided observation tasks, helping beginners understand what they are viewing and record their own findings.

What it does and how it works

Users explore a regional map and independently switch layers for observation materials, simulated routes, illustrative hazards, and personal notes. The application brings together imagery from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Perseverance rover, with a regional basemap derived from ESA’s Mars Express mission.

P1 introduces a Perseverance photograph taken from Octavia E. Butler Landing and distinguishes the camera location from the distant delta feature shown in the image. A separate delta-front observation area provides orbital context and access to Skinner Ridge and Wildcat Ridge materials. Users can inspect rock layers, mark visible features, compare close-up textures, and save written observations. Task completion requires a separate user confirmation.

Three preset routes demonstrate simulated travel to STP1, a clearly labeled demonstration destination. Users can also create custom waypoints and optional tasks. Browser storage preserves observations and journey progress, while a text export lets users keep their mission logs.

Benefits and intended impact

MarsPath aims to make Mars exploration more approachable for students and curious members of the public. Instead of presenting photographs as isolated images, it places them within a wider exploration experience and encourages users to look closely, describe evidence, and compare observations.

The intended impact is educational: supporting curiosity about planetary science while helping users distinguish direct visual observations from scientific interpretations and simulated scenarios.

Tools and development

We built the application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with SVG for map overlays and interactive markers. It runs in a desktop web browser without requiring a backend, database, account, or API key for the mission experience. Development and browser testing took place on Windows using Chrome. AI assistance supported coding, debugging, and documentation, while the team reviewed the interface, selected materials, and tested interactions.

Creative approach

The project combines a mission simulation with an image-based observation notebook. Users can plan a journey, explore scientific photographs, and leave their own records within one interface. Independent layers help keep different kinds of information understandable, while custom routes allow users to design their own demonstration activities.

Factors we considered

We prioritized source attribution, beginner accessibility, and a clear distinction between authentic imagery and simulated content. Image records retain source information and distinguish capture dates from publication dates where available.

We also considered geographic uncertainty. P1 has an approximate display position, and the delta-front area represents broad context rather than a surveyed boundary. We do not assign verified individual map coordinates to Skinner Ridge or Wildcat Ridge.

Routes, hazards, and travel metrics are illustrative. MarsPath does not provide validated navigation or real-time environmental conditions. Future development would focus on geographic registration, terrain-based route validation, and broader browser and touch-device testing.
